newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees 1997 consumer inflation at 4.0 percent.
newsitem.headline: China sees 1997 consumer inflation at 4.0 percent.

text.p: China's galloping inflation will slow to a snail's pace in 1997 although sharp rises in service costs, rather than traditional index-heavy foodstuffs, are fuelling the consumer price index, an official said on Friday.

China's benchmark retail price index was seen rising two percent for all of 1997, with the consumer price index -- which includes services -- up four percent, said Ren Caifang, a statistician with the State Statistical Bureau.
"With economic growth staying within a suitable zone, prices will continue to appear stable and it is not likely that there will be a large rebound," Ren told reporters at a briefing.

Inflation had slowed largely due to sliding grain prices, which weigh heavily in the indices and which fell a year-on-year 4.2 percent in the first half of 1997 after two consecutive bumper harvests, Ren said.
China's retail inflation was a year-on-year 1.8 percent in the first half while the consumer price index rose 4.1 percent in the period.
Retail inflation was 6.1 percent last year, down from 14.8 percent in 1995 and a communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994.
"The price of grain has been falling for the past six to seven months," Ren said, adding that prices of meat and fresh vegetables had also dropped. "This is a pretty good trend."

China does not specify what is in the basket of items that make up the two indices or their exact weightings, but analysts say the consumer index is a broader measure than the retail index because it includes services.
Beijing has said it will eventually use the consumer index as its benchmark figure.

Ren shed some light on China's secretive statistical methods, saying prices for food, which analysts say makes up more than 40 percent of people's expenditures, rose 1.4 percent in the first half, accounting for 16.1 percent of the consumer index rise.
In the past, increases in food prices accounted for 40-70 percent of consumer price inflation, Ren said without elaborating.
Initial estimates put China's summer grain harvest at 123.95 million tonnes, an increase of 10.75 million tonnes from last year.
The Ministry of Internal Trade has forecast grain output for the year at more than 484 million tonnes, compared with a record 490 million tonnes in 1996.
Housing prices rose 9.8 percent in the first half while the cost of services jumped 17.6 percent, with the two categories making up 60.9 percent of the rise in the consumer price index, Ren said.
Within those categories, postal prices rocketed 112.1 percent, rents increased 23.6 percent and health services rose 21.6 percent, he said.
Despite Beijing's tight credit policy aimed at reining in inflation, China's economy grew strongly in the first half, rising by 9.5 percent in the period compared with 9.7 percent for all of 1996.
